Subject: Latency acceptance heuristics & next steps (CrowdBank)

Jordan — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps focused on the p95/p99 E2E targets we discussed. Attaching the traffic envelope and a short prompt set for Redwood's test harness.

Call recap (high level):
- Goal: confirm whether Redwood hosted API can meet CrowdBank's E2E latency SLOs for short conversational requests and streaming responses.
- Current provider: CrowdBank reported intermittent p99 spikes around 1.2s under production bursts (short prompts, ~256 tokens).
- CrowdBank target: p95 <= 200 ms, p99 <= 500 ms for typical single-turn requests (including network hop to provider region).
- Throughput/traffic envelope: sustained 30 RPS with short bursts to 120 RPS; expected concurrency ~50 active sessions.
- Streaming: chunked partial responses used in the UI; tail behavior during streaming is a primary concern.

What Redwood needs from CrowdBank to run a representative test:
1) Sample traffic envelope (attached: crowdbank-traffic-envelope.csv).
2) Representative prompt set (attached: crowdbank-prompt-set.txt) including the top 40 prompts by frequency.
3) Short window to run a controlled bakeoff (2x 30-minute windows during off-peak).
4) If possible, a short-lived service account or pre-signed endpoints so we can run tests from a client routing similar to your prod path (we can also run from our EU/US region if you prefer).

Redwood proposition / test plan (proposal):
- Phase A (lab): Redwood runs 30 min baseline tests on hosted API (identical model variant) using your envelope. Goal: measure p95/p99 for short prompts (<=256 tokens), with and without streaming enabled.
- Phase B (burst): Simulate bursts to 120 RPS to observe tail behavior and backpressure.
- Phase C (canary): If Phase A/B look good, run a short canary with 15-30 min live traffic mirror (if you can support).

Practical constraints & clarifications:
- Tokenization and model variant matter — we'll match your current model family if available in Redwood's catalog; if not, we'll pick a close equivalent and note differences.
- Network overhead (client -> CrowdBank -> Redwood) will affect absolute numbers; we'll include simple network RTT baselining in the report.

Next steps I propose:
- Jordan: confirm the sample files are correct and share a suitable test window (we suggested next week).
- Ben: please review the perf knobs we should try by default and any data collection hooks to include in the test harness.
- Marissa: I'll need a short note on pricing for a test that requires dedicated slot time / reserved capacity if the customer insists on production-like isolation.

Attachments: crowdbank-traffic-envelope.csv (CSV), crowdbank-prompt-set.txt (TXT)

Thanks — Diego

--

Thanks Diego — nice summary. A few technical notes / baseline checklist I recommend we include in Phase A so the bakeoff yields actionable results:

Baseline test config (proposed):
- Model & sequence: match to 1) typical prompt lengths (median ~120 tokens), 2) worst-case short (~16 tokens) and long (~512 tokens) buckets. p95/p99 are most meaningful for the short path here.
- Measurement: end-to-end elapsed time measured at the client (includes client -> Redwood network RTT), plus server-side per-token breakdown (server queueing, decode time, kernel run).
- Batching policy: run with continuous batching turned off, then on with 20ms hold to see cost/latency tradeoff.
- KV cache warm/cold: include runs with cache cold and warm; streaming/partial output often benefits from warm KV.
- Concurrency shaping: sustain 30 RPS (steady-state) for 30 min; run 3x 2-min spikes to 120 RPS to observe tail.
- Streaming specifics: use chunk sizes matching CrowdBank client (they mentioned 64-256 byte chunks). We'll measure tail latency defined as time to first chunk (TTFC) and time between last token and last chunk.

Data collection:
- We'll publish an artifacts bundle with: raw client timings, server-side histograms (p50/p95/p99), and a short runbook of observed failure modes.
- If CrowdBank can expose CloudFront/Edge logs (or their loadbalancer timings) we can align events. Otherwise we'll provide a reference harness and ask CrowdBank to run their side once.

Operational recommendations (quick):
- If we see p99 > 500 ms under your envelope, first check network RTT and long-tail kernel stalls. Quantization sometimes increases variance; prefer q4f16 or similar conservative profile for production.
- If streaming tail is the issue, consider: smaller model foot and aggressive per-chunk flushing, or a slightly larger first-chunk model to get TTFC down.

I'll prepare a short test config and a minimal script for the harness (we can host it in that Drive folder Diego linked).

— Ben
